summary: William Kantrowitz complains again, following RFC 459, about the many requests for information that ARPANET sites receive, such as host charts that duplicate the Resource Notebook and requests for hourly load numbers. It is an opinion piece. It updates RFC 459.

eli5.summary: A grumble about people sending too many requests for information that waste everyone's time and double the paperwork.

subtitle: A TX-2 engineer protests the pile of information requests landing on small ARPANET sites.

tldr.problem: ARPANET sites keep receiving requests for charts, load figures, and program listings, and small research sites like TX-2 risk getting nothing done while answering them.
tldr.mechanism: W. Kantrowitz lists three recent examples, asks pointed questions about a request for listings of every program, repeats his plea from RFC 459, and asks requesters to justify their requests before sending them.
tldr.outcome: It is an opinion piece with no protocol. It updates RFC 459, and RFC 531 responds to it.

today: The unit metadata lists this RFC's status as Unknown and records no replacement. It updates RFC 459, and RFC 531 is a response to it.

sections.title: Three Recent Annoyances
sections.content: Kantrowitz says the ARPA Network has drawn out "compulsive collectors and organizers". He gives three examples. First, a set of charts on host characteristics called the "ARPA Network handbook", which scatters information on a host over many pages and duplicates much of the Resource Notebook, so two documents must be maintained. Second, a telephone call asking for hourly loads on the TX-2 computer for every hour of April and May. Third, a mailbox message about a "central software repository" and a personnel file, which he calls the immediate precursor of this RFC.
sections.eli5: People kept asking for charts, numbers and lists that nobody really needed, and each one meant extra work.

sections.title: The Program Listings Request
sections.content:
The RFC addresses only the idea of listings of every program. Kantrowitz asks how much paper this would produce, how many filing cabinets it would need, who would use the result, and whether a new listing would have to be sent for every program change. For TX-2, many programs are written in assembly language, so he asks whether the site should also send its incomplete assembly language manual or its operating system listings.

The attached message from RML at USC-ISI asks host sites to send copies of advertised programs with documentation (description, listings, running instructions, limitations) to the Range Measurements Laboratory. It also asks for a file of staff with particular technical talents.
sections.eli5: He asks silly-sounding but fair questions, like how many trees would be cut down for all that paper.

sections.title: The Plea
sections.content:
Kantrowitz repeats his plea from RFC 459: small research sites such as TX-2 should not be drowned in make-work. He recalls that in the mid 1960s TX-2 was able to get something done, including early experiments with a small-scale network prototype with SDC that helped lead to the ARPA Network.

He ends with advice for the next requester. Think hard about the justification, consider how long the work will take others, explain why they should be motivated, write that down as the introduction to the "work order", and try it on colleagues first.
sections.eli5: His advice is to ask whether a request is worth other people's time before you send it.

references.text: Kantrowitz, W., RFC 459, the earlier plea referred to in this RFC.
T. Marill and L. Roberts, "Toward a Cooperative Network of Time-Shared Computers", AFIPS Conference Proceedings, November 1966.
